headline: Montauk runs blind into June as buoy network goes quiet and data gaps widen
subhead: With offshore stations 44017 and 44025 offline and no current SST overlay, the Point's early-summer pattern has to be read from structure and seasonality alone.
body_markdown:
The Point is fishing in the dark this week, at least from a data standpoint. The Dr. Fish analyst feed came back essentially empty today — no live buoy readings posted for the region, no current sea-surface temperature package beyond the June 8 catalog entry, and the offshore sentinels we lean on hardest at this time of year are all flagged offline: 44017 south of Montauk, 44025 off the south shore, and the canyon-approach stations 44039 and 44040. Wind data at 44097 and 44091 is also missing. That means no hard number to put on Block Island Sound surface temps, no confirmed thermal break position east of the Point, and no real-time sea state off Shagwong. What we do have is the calendar: June 10, a week past the new moon, sitting in the heart of the early-season transition when bottom water in the Sound is climbing through the mid-50s and the south side ocean is generally a few degrees behind.

In a normal year on this date, that thermal split is the entire story for the beat. Cooler, cleaner water riding the south side from the Lighthouse west to Turtle Cove holds the heaviest early bass, while the warmer water funneling out of Gardiners and Block Island Sound on the dropping tide loads bait against North Bar and Shagwong. Without the SST overlay to confirm where that edge sits this week, the safe read is to fish the structure as if the break is tight to the beach — meaning the boulder field from the Lighthouse west, the rip line off the Point on the dropping east tide, and the inside edge of North Bar on the last of the flood. Fluke should be settling into their post-spawn pattern on the south side drops in 40 to 60 feet, and the porgy push into Fort Pond Bay and the rockpiles off Shagwong is on schedule.

On-the-ground intelligence is thinner than I'd like. The party boat and charter feed that normally tells us when the south side fluke drift turns on has not been refreshed, and the inshore reports filtering in describe a single bay trip rather than a fleet pattern. What is consistent with the season is that the bass bite at the Point this week should be a tide-and-tackle game rather than a numbers game — the trophy class fish that stage on the Point in early June are there, but they require live eels drifted in the rip after dark on the dropping tide, or large soft plastics worked slowly through the boulder field at first light. The blitz-and-burn topwater window most anglers associate with Montauk is still six to eight weeks out.

Bluefish should be scattered through the Sound and along the south side beaches, with the first real gator class fish showing on the troll between the Lighthouse and Block. Fluke drifts on the south side have historically come alive in the second week of June once the water clears post-spawn, and the calendar says we are right on that hinge. Bucktail and Gulp on a long drift in 45 to 55 feet from Turtle Cove west should produce keepers, with the larger fish favoring the slower drifts on the lighter tides — which the moon phase is giving us for the next several days.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variables I would watch are wind direction and the eventual return of the buoy and SST feeds. A sustained southwest breeze, which is the climatological default for mid-June, will stack bait against the Lighthouse on the dropping tide and is the single best setup for a quality bass bite from the rocks. Any easterly component dirties the south side and pushes the program north to Shagwong and the Sound. New moon energy is fading, so tides will moderate through the week — favorable for fluke drifts, slightly less favorable for the heaviest current-driven bass bite at the Point. If the SST package refreshes and shows the offshore break tightening inside 30 fathoms, the bonito and early albie conversation starts earlier than usual; if it stays cool, hold the line on bass and bottom.

The honest report this morning is that Montauk is fishing on its seasonal script with the instrument panel half dark. The Point does not stop producing because a buoy goes offline, and the structure here rewards anglers who read tide and wind before they read a screen. Fish the dropping tide hard at the Lighthouse, work the south side drops for fluke on the softer tides this week, and keep an eye on Shagwong if the wind turns east.
